reference.source: Brukner and Khan's Clinical Sports Medicine
clinicalPearls: Medial elbow pain from the common flexor-pronator origin, a degenerative tendinopathy rather than a true inflammation
Provoked by resisted wrist flexion and forearm pronation, and by gripping
Tenderness localises to the medial epicondyle and just distal to it
The ulnar nerve lies close by and may be irritated or entrapped, so ulnar nerve symptoms should be sought
Diagnosis is largely clinical, with imaging (ultrasound or MRI) reserved for uncertain or refractory cases

Management mirrors lateral epicondylitis with activity modification, progressive or eccentric loading and physiotherapy, and cautious use of corticosteroid injection given tendon and nearby ulnar nerve considerations
reference.pathophysiology: Medial epicondylitis is an overuse tendinopathy of the common flexor-pronator origin at the medial humeral epicondyle, arising from repetitive wrist flexion, forearm pronation and gripping loads, as in golf and throwing or racquet sports. As with other chronic tendinopathies the pathology is degenerative, with disorganised collagen, mucoid change and neovascularisation and little inflammation, reflecting failed tendon healing under repetitive load. The proximity of the ulnar nerve within the cubital tunnel means concurrent ulnar neuropathy is not uncommon.
additionalDifferentials: Ulnar neuropathy at the elbow (cubital tunnel syndrome)
Ulnar collateral ligament injury or insufficiency
Referred pain from the shoulder or neck
additionalInvestigations: Clinical provocative tests (resisted wrist flexion and pronation, palpation of the medial epicondyle)
Assessment of ulnar nerve function (Tinel's sign over the cubital tunnel, sensory testing)
Ultrasound to confirm common flexor tendinopathy
MRI in unclear or refractory cases and to assess the ulnar collateral ligament
Nerve conduction studies if ulnar neuropathy is suspected
redFlags: Ulnar nerve symptoms such as little and ring finger numbness or intrinsic weakness suggesting neuropathy
Valgus instability suggesting collateral ligament failure
Systemic features or night pain suggesting other pathology
Failure to respond, prompting review of the diagnosis
reference.prognosis: Most improve with load management and progressive rehabilitation, although recovery may be slow; coexisting ulnar neuropathy or ligament injury can complicate the course.
pitfalls: Corticosteroid injection risking tendon harm and ulnar nerve injury if poorly placed
Treating as inflammatory rather than a loading problem
Missing ulnar collateral ligament injury in throwing athletes
references: Brukner and Khan's Clinical Sports Medicine
management: Activity modification and load management to offload the flexor-pronator origin
Progressive loading and eccentric rehabilitation of the flexor-pronator muscles as the mainstay
Short-term analgesia with NSAIDs and ice, plus counterforce bracing and correction of technique and ergonomics
Assess for and manage coexisting ulnar neuropathy
Consider a corticosteroid injection for short-term symptom relief in refractory cases, weighing its limited long-term benefit
Surgical debridement of the degenerate tendon reserved for cases refractory to prolonged conservative care
Counsel the patient that recovery is often slow
